title: "Movement data & the aniframe"
description: "Meet the aniframe — the tidy data structure every animovement package reads and returns."
order: 2
---

Every *animovement* package speaks the same language: the **aniframe**. It's the
data structure defined by [anicore](https://animovement.dev/anicore) that
readers return, processing functions transform, and plotting functions
visualise. Understand it once, and the whole ecosystem clicks into place.

## What is an aniframe? {#sec-what}

An aniframe is a [tibble](https://tibble.tidyverse.org) with some extra
structure. It stays *tidy* — one observation per row — and it carries metadata
about your recording. Because it's a tibble underneath, every `dplyr`, `tidyr`
and `ggplot2` trick you already know works on it.

Each row answers three questions:

| Question | Slot | Default columns |
|----------|------|-----------------|
| **What** is moving? | `variables_what` | `individual`, `keypoint` |
| **When**? | `variables_when` | `session`, `trial`, `time` |
| **Where**? | `variables_where` | `x`, `y` (and `z` in 3-D) |

The *what* and *when* columns together form a key that uniquely identifies each
row; the *where* columns hold the measured position. Pose-estimation data also
carries a `confidence` column — how sure the tracker was about each point.

## A first look {#sec-look}

The quickest way to see one is `example_aniframe()`, which simulates a small
dataset for you:

```r
library(animovement)

movement <- example_aniframe(
  n_individuals = 2,
  n_keypoints = 3,
  n_obs = 100
)

movement
```

Printing an aniframe shows a short header summarising *what* it contains,
followed by the tidy table:

```
# Individuals: 1, 2
# Keypoints:   head, neck, shoulder_right
# Sessions:    1
# Trials:      1
   individual keypoint        session trial  time       x        y confidence
        <int> <fct>             <int> <int> <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>
 1          1 head                  1     1     1 -1.31    -0.771       0.929
 2          1 head                  1     1     2  0.0531   1.22        0.380
 3          1 head                  1     1     3  0.915   -0.532       0.645
 # … with many more rows
```

The `#` header lines are the summary; the columns below map straight onto the
*what / when / where* slots from the table above.

## Create one from your own data {#sec-create}

Most of the time you won't build an aniframe by hand — a
[reader](read-data.qmd) does it for you. But when your data is already in a
plain data frame, `as_aniframe()` casts it, and you tell it which columns fill
which slot:

```r
df <- data.frame(
  track = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4),  # which animal
  time  = rep(1:4, 2),                 # when
  x     = runif(8),                    # where
  y     = runif(8)
)

movement <- as_aniframe(
  df,
  variables_what = "track",   # identity lives in `track`, not `individual`
  variables_when = "time"
)
```

If your columns already use the default names (`individual`, `keypoint`,
`time`, `x`, `y`), you can drop the arguments entirely: `as_aniframe(df)`.

To build one directly from vectors, use `aniframe()`:

```r
aniframe(
  individual = rep(1:2, each = 25),
  time       = rep(1:10, 5),
  x          = rnorm(50),
  y          = rnorm(50)
)
```

Check whether any object is an aniframe with `is_aniframe()`.

## Metadata: units, sampling rate, origin {#sec-metadata}

An aniframe remembers context that a bare data frame would lose — the sampling
rate, the units of space and time, where the coordinate origin sits. Set these
so downstream calculations (speeds, distances) come out in meaningful units:

```r
movement <- movement |>
  set_sampling_rate(30) |>       # frames per second
  set_unit_time("s") |>
  set_unit_space("mm")

get_metadata(movement)
```

## Events: the anievent {#sec-anievent}

Alongside the aniframe, *anicore* defines the **anievent** — a companion
structure for *labelled events* rather than continuous tracks (think behavioural
annotations: "grooming from t = 12 to t = 20", or a point event at a single
frame). You'll meet it when you work with annotation exports such as
[BORIS](read-data.qmd); create one with `anievent()` or derive it from per-frame
data with `to_anievent()`.
